mentions.quote: only here may animals be slain, and nowhere else, Manu has declared.
the meat of an animal killed by dogs, Manu has declared to be pure
these Svayambhuva Manu has declared to be the bowls of an ascetic

entities.description: Manu (also called Svayambhuva Manu) is the primordial lawgiver whose declarations constitute the authoritative rulings throughout this text on ritual purity and conduct.
entities.justification: Manu is cited as the direct source of legal pronouncements on animal slaughter, purity rules, and ascetic implements across multiple verses in p-89d810.

mentions.quote: for they are always in the state of Indra and have become one with Brahma
A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.

entities.description: Indra is the king of the gods, listed as one of the eight world-protectors whose combined form constitutes the divine essence of a king.
entities.justification: Indra appears in p-89d810 both as a divine state that kings embody and as one of the eight lords whose qualities compose royal nature.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.

entities.description: Soma is a Vedic deity and one of the eight world-protectors whose collective form is said to be embodied in a king.
entities.justification: Soma is explicitly named in p-89d810 as one of the eight divine lords whose combined qualities constitute the nature of a king.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.

entities.description: Agni, the fire deity, is one of the eight world-protectors whose collective form constitutes the divine nature of kingship.
entities.justification: Agni is explicitly named in p-89d810 as one of the eight divine lords composing the king's form.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.

entities.description: Varuna, the lord of waters and cosmic order, is one of the eight world-protectors embodied in a king.
entities.justification: Varuna is identified as 'lord of waters' in p-89d810 as one of the eight divine constituents of royal nature.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.
He should reflect on the states of men, which arise from the faults of their actions, and on their fall into hell, and the torments in the abode of Yama.

entities.description: Yama is the god of death and lord of the underworld whose abode is a place of torment for the sinful, and who also constitutes one of the eight world-protectors forming the nature of a king.
entities.justification: Yama appears in p-89d810 both as the lord of the death realm where sinners are tormented and as one of the eight divine lords that compose a king's nature.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.

entities.description: Kubera, the lord of wealth and guardian of the north, is one of the eight world-protectors whose combined form constitutes kingship.
entities.justification: Kubera is identified as 'lord of wealth' in p-89d810 as one of the eight divine constituents of a king's nature.

mentions.quote: For the sake of auspiciousness, the rite of well-being and the sacrifice to Prajapati are performed for them at marriage, but the giving away is the cause of ownership.
Having performed the Prajapatya sacrifice, with all his wealth as the sacrificial fee, having placed the sacred fires within himself, a Brahmana should go forth from his house as a renouncer.

entities.description: Prajapati is the Lord of Creatures to whom the marriage sacrifice and the final Prajapatya sacrifice are offered as key transitional rites.
entities.justification: Prajapati is named in p-89d810 as the deity of the marriage sacrifice and of the Prajapatya sacrifice performed at the transition to renunciation.

mentions.quote: for they are always in the state of Indra and have become one with Brahma
For him who goes forth from his house as a renouncer, having given a promise of safety to all beings, there are worlds of light, say the expounders of Brahma.
A Brahmana who has cast off his body by one of these practices of the great sages, being free from sorrow and fear, is exalted in the world of Brahma.
By this rule, having gradually abandoned all attachments, freed from all pairs of opposites, he becomes established in Brahma alone.
That twice-born who becomes a renouncer by this orderly method, he, having shaken off his sin here, attains the supreme Brahma.
by the yoga of meditation he goes to the eternal Brahma.

entities.description: Brahma (here the Absolute/Ultimate Reality rather than the creator deity Brahma) is the supreme final state attained through renunciation, meditation, and the tenfold Dharma.
entities.justification: Brahma appears repeatedly across p-89d810, p-79fcf5, p-45027a, and p-1270ce as the ultimate destination of the renouncer who follows prescribed Dharma.

mentions.quote: Having touched a Chandala, a menstruating woman, an outcaste, a woman who has just given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one is purified by bathing.
The meat of an animal killed by dogs, Manu has declared to be pure, and that killed by other carnivorous animals, and by Chandalas and other robbers.

entities.description: Chandalas are the lowest-caste group in the varna hierarchy, whose touch causes ritual impurity but whose killing of animals paradoxically does not render the meat impure.
entities.justification: Chandalas appear in p-89d810 as both transmitters of ritual impurity through touch and as agents whose animal-kills yield ritually pure meat.

mentions.quote: Or he may live always on flowers, roots, and fruits alone, which have ripened in time and fallen of their own accord, abiding in the rule of the Vaikhanasas.

entities.description: The Vaikhanasas are an ascetic tradition or school whose rule of living solely on naturally fallen plant matter is presented as a valid forest-dwelling practice.
entities.justification: The Vaikhanasas are cited in p-89d810 as an established tradition whose dietary rule the forest-dweller may optionally follow.

mentions.quote: Through infidelity to her husband, a woman obtains condemnation in the world; she obtains the womb of a jackal and is afflicted by sinful diseases.

entities.description: The jackal is the animal into whose womb an adulterous woman is reborn as karmic punishment for infidelity.
entities.justification: The jackal womb is named in p-89d810 as the specific rebirth destination of a woman who commits infidelity against her husband.

mentions.quote: As a tree on a riverbank, or as a bird on a tree, so he who abandons this body is freed from the crocodile of suffering.

entities.description: The crocodile is used as a metaphor for the suffering of embodied existence from which the renouncer is freed upon abandoning the body.
entities.justification: In p-9931a5 the crocodile figures as an image of saṃsāric suffering in a simile comparing the renouncer's liberation to a bird leaving a tree.

mentions.quote: A Brahmana dwelling in the forest should observe these and other vows, and various Upanishadic texts from the Śruti for the perfection of his soul.
He should constantly recite the sacred texts relating to sacrifice, to the deities, and to the Self, and that which is declared in the Vedanta.
A twice-born, having practiced this tenfold Dharma with a concentrated mind, and having duly heard the Vedanta, should renounce, being free from his debts.

entities.description: The Vedanta (Upanishads), as part of the Śruti, is the scriptural corpus that forest-dwellers and renouncers must study for spiritual perfection and as a prerequisite to renunciation.
entities.justification: Vedanta/Upanishadic texts appear as prescribed study material in p-89d810, p-c29fdd, and p-2d97a0, constituting a key element of the forest-dweller and renouncer stages.

mentions.quote: He should also offer the Agnihotra from the three sacred fires according to the rule, not omitting the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices at the proper time.

entities.description: The Agnihotra is the daily fire-oblation that the forest-dwelling hermit must continue to perform from the three sacred fires according to rule.
entities.justification: The Agnihotra is explicitly prescribed in p-89d810 as a mandatory daily rite the forest-dweller must maintain even in renunciate life.

mentions.quote: Having performed the Prajapatya sacrifice, with all his wealth as the sacrificial fee, having placed the sacred fires within himself, a Brahmana should go forth from his house as a renouncer.

entities.description: The Prajapatya sacrifice is the final sacrificial rite, performed with all one's wealth as the sacrificial fee, that marks the Brahmana's transition from householder to renouncer.
entities.justification: The Prajapatya sacrifice is named in p-89d810 as the prescribed ritual act that precedes going forth as a renouncer.

mentions.quote: Or he may live according to the rules of the Chandrayana penance during the bright and dark fortnights; or at the end of the fortnights, he may eat boiled gruel once.

entities.description: The Chandrayana penance is a lunar-cycle-based fasting practice that the forest-dweller may optionally follow as a form of bodily austerity.
entities.justification: The Chandrayana penance is mentioned in p-89d810 as one valid ascetic dietary regime for the forest-dweller stage.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.
if it is without fat, by sipping water, or by touching a cow or looking at the sun
when he is pure, recite mantras to the sun according to his zeal

entities.description: Arka/the Sun is simultaneously one of the eight world-protectors constituting royal nature, a purifying agent for a Brahmana who touches a bone, and the recipient of mantras recited upon encountering impure persons.
entities.justification: The Sun appears in p-89d810 in three distinct ritual functions: as a constituent of kingship, as a purificatory sight, and as the addressee of protective mantras.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.
Flies, drops of spittle, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun, dust, the earth, wind, and fire—these one should know to be pure in contact.

entities.description: Anila/Wind is one of the eight world-protectors forming the divine nature of a king, and wind is also listed as a substance that is pure upon contact.
entities.justification: Anila/wind appears in p-89d810 both as a constituent of the divine kingship formula and as one of the naturally pure elements.

mentions.quote: Among sapiṇḍas, a ten-day period of impurity from a death is prescribed; but if it is before the gathering of the bones, it may be for three days, or for one day only.
A Brahmana is purified in ten days, a ruler in twelve days, a Vaishya in fifteen days, and a Shudra is purified in a month.
Knowledge, tapas, fire, food, earth, mind, water, plastering with cow-dung, wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents of purification for embodied beings.

themes.justification: The bulk of chapter 06 (Manusmṛti 5.57–5.145) systematically legislates periods and methods of purification after death, birth, and contact with impure substances, constituting the chapter's dominant theme.

mentions.quote: A twice-born snātaka, having thus dwelt in the householder āśrama according to the rule, should dwell in the forest, self-controlled and with his senses duly conquered.
When a householder sees wrinkles and gray hair on his body, and the child of his own child, then he should take refuge in the forest.
The celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic—these four separate āśramas originate from the householder.
And of all these, according to the ordinance of the Veda and the Smṛti, the householder is declared to be the most excellent, for he supports these other three.

themes.justification: Manusmṛti 6.1–6.97 structures the second half of the chapter around the progressive movement through the four āśramas, describing duties at each stage and ranking the householder as supreme.

mentions.quote: Having discharged his three debts, he should fix his mind on liberation (mokṣa); but he who pursues mokṣa without having discharged them, sinks downwards.
That twice-born who becomes a renouncer by this orderly method, he, having shaken off his sin here, attains the supreme Brahma.
By this rule, having gradually abandoned all attachments, freed from all pairs of opposites, he becomes established in Brahma alone.

themes.justification: The forest-dweller and renouncer sections (6.33–6.97) focus on mokṣa as the culminating goal, with detailed conditions and practices for valid renunciation culminating in union with Brahma.

themes.topic: Dharma of women and wifely subordination

mentions.quote: By a girl, by a young woman, or even by an aged woman, nothing must be done independently, even in her own house.
In childhood, she must be under the control of her father; in youth, of her husband; when her husband is dead, of her sons; a woman must never enjoy independence.
For women, there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor any fasting; by the service she renders her husband, by that she is exalted in heaven.

themes.justification: Manusmṛti 5.147–5.168 constitutes a distinct section on strīdharma (women's duty) prescribing total subordination to male relatives across every life stage.

themes.topic: Non-violence (ahiṃsā) and the ethics of meat-eating

mentions.quote: He who does not wish to cause confinement, death, or pain to living beings, he, desiring the welfare of all, enjoys supreme happiness.
Without having done violence to living beings, meat is nowhere produced; and the killing of a living being is not conducive to heaven; therefore, one should avoid meat.
There is no sin in the eating of meat, nor in wine, nor in sexual union; this is the natural inclination (pravṛtti) of beings, but abstention (nivṛtti) yields great fruit.

themes.justification: Manusmṛti 5.41–5.56 opens the chapter with a sustained argument on the ethics of meat-eating, balancing Vedic sanction for ritual slaughter against the superior merit of abstention.

themes.topic: Tapas (austerity) as purification and spiritual power

mentions.quote: In summer, he should perform the five-fires penance; during the rains, he should live under the open sky; and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, gradually increasing his tapas.
The learned are purified by forbearance; doers of forbidden acts, by giving; those with secret sins, by recitation; and the best knowers of the Veda, by tapas.
Even three suppressions of the breath, performed according to the rule by a Brahmana, accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the syllable Om, are to be known as the highest tapas.

themes.justification: Tapas pervades the forest-dweller and renouncer sections (6.6–6.75) as the primary means of burning away sin, purifying the senses, and advancing toward liberation.

mentions.quote: He should reflect on the states of men, which arise from the faults of their actions, and on their fall into hell, and the torments in the abode of Yama.
Through infidelity to her husband, a woman obtains condemnation in the world; she obtains the womb of a jackal and is afflicted by sinful diseases.
And on the departure from this body, and the rebirth in a womb, and the passages of this inner soul through thousands of millions of wombs.

themes.justification: The text repeatedly invokes karmic consequence — hellish torment, animal rebirth, and transmigration through innumerable wombs — as motivating framework for following prescribed Dharma.

themes.topic: Varna hierarchy and differential ritual obligations

mentions.quote: A Brahmana is purified in ten days, a ruler in twelve days, a Vaishya in fifteen days, and a Shudra is purified in a month.
One should carry out a deceased Shudra through the southern gate of the town; but the twice-born, through the western, northern, or eastern gates, as is appropriate.
He who wishes to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another, without having worshipped the ancestors and the gods—there is no one more unmeritorious than he.

themes.justification: The differential purity periods, funeral rites, and ritual obligations assigned to each varna throughout the chapter reflect a structuring principle that varna determines the form and duration of all ritual obligations.

mentions.quote: A king bears the form of the eight world-protectors: Soma, Agni, Arka (the Sun), Anila (the Wind), Indra, the lord of wealth (Kubera), the lord of waters (Varuna), and Yama.
There is no fault of impurity for kings, nor for those under a vow, nor for those engaged in a sacrificial session; for they are always in the state of Indra and have become one with Brahma.
A king is established by the lords of the world, so no impurity is prescribed for him; for the purity and impurity of mortals arise from and are resolved by the lords of the world.

themes.justification: Manusmṛti 5.93–5.98 presents kingship as ontologically divine — the king embodies eight world-protectors and therefore stands above ordinary purity rules, a rare political-theology passage in the chapter.

themes.topic: Yoga and meditation (dhyāna) as inner technology

mentions.quote: He should burn away his faults with suppressions of the breath, his sin with concentrations, his worldly attachments with withdrawal of the senses, and his ungodly qualities with meditation.
By the yoga of meditation, he should perceive the course of this inner soul in high and low beings, which is difficult to know for those whose souls are unpurified.
By the yoga of meditation, he should perceive the course of this inner soul in high and low beings, which is difficult to know for those whose souls are unpurified.
by the yoga of meditation he goes to the eternal Brahma.

themes.justification: Manusmṛti 6.70–6.79 introduces a systematic inner technology of prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, and dhyāna as the renouncer's path to perceiving the ātman and attaining Brahma.

themes.topic: Three debts and preconditions for renunciation

mentions.quote: Having discharged his three debts, he should fix his mind on liberation (mokṣa); but he who pursues mokṣa without having discharged them, sinks downwards.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rule, having begotten sons according to Dharma, and having sacrificed with yajñas according to his ability, he should fix his mind on liberation.

themes.justification: The three debts — to teachers (Veda-study), to ancestors (sons), and to gods (sacrifice) — are implicit as the prerequisite structure for renunciation in 6.35–6.37, named collectively but unpacked across verses.

citations.quote: The violence which is sanctioned by the Veda and is established in this movable and immovable world, one should know to be non-violence itself; for Dharma shone forth from the Veda.
citations.justification: The Veda is cited as the ultimate authority from which Dharma derives, validating ritual violence (animal sacrifice) as non-violence when Vedically sanctioned.

citations.quote: A self-possessed twice-born, dwelling in his house, with his guru, or in the forest, must not perform violence not sanctioned by the Veda, even in a time of distress.
citations.justification: The Veda is invoked as the standard against which all ritual action is measured, making non-Vedic violence impermissible even under duress.

citations.quote: And of all these, according to the ordinance of the Veda and the Smṛti, the householder is declared to be the most excellent, for he supports these other three.
citations.justification: The Smṛti is cited alongside the Veda as a co-authoritative source for the ranking of the householder stage above the other three āśramas.

citations.quote: A Brahmana dwelling in the forest should observe these and other vows, and various Upanishadic texts from the Śruti for the perfection of his soul.
citations.justification: The Upanishadic texts are cited as authoritative Śruti whose study is prescribed for the forest-dweller's spiritual perfection.
